title: Patrick's Confession
hook: Patrick calls himself a sinner, most rustic, and tells his story humbly
tomorrow: a prayer you put on like armor. what is it guarding?

segments.voice: Yesterday a Highland kitchen lit its fire with a flame of love for the foe too: kindle the fire. Today, the hardest story to tell well: your own.

Every profile asks for the best version: three lines, best angle, wins only. How do you tell your own story without making yourself the hero? Patrick had a story built for bragging. Taken by raiders, held captive, escaped, and later back in the very land that held him. Here's how he starts it: “Ego Patricius peccator rusticissimus.” I, Patrick, a sinner, most rustic.
screen: `WINS ONLY.` → `A STORY BUILT FOR BRAGGING.` → `I, PATRICK, A SINNER.`

segments.voice: He keeps lowering himself as he goes: the least of all the faithful, looked down on by many, his Latin rough, written by someone who never studied the way others did. So why write at all? Because, he says, it would be wrong to keep quiet about the gifts God gave him in the land of his captivity. His best picture: before he was humbled, he was like a stone lying deep in the mud, and he that is mighty came and in his mercy lifted him up and set him on top of the wall. The order matters. First, I am a sinner. Then, look what God did. Paul writes it the same way to Timothy: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” A neighbor tradition says something close. The Buddhist Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation: “The fool who knows his foolishness, is wise at least so far. But a fool who thinks himself wise, he is called a fool indeed.” Both treat an honest look at your own lack as the place wisdom starts. The difference is real. Patrick's story turns on mercy: a mighty one reaches into the mud and lifts. The Dhammapada's verse is about seeing clearly, and elsewhere it says you must make the effort yourself; the Buddhas only show the way. Shared: the honest start. Different: who does the lifting.
screen: `THE LEAST OF ALL THE FAITHFUL.` · `A STONE LIFTED FROM THE MUD.` · `THE FOOL WHO KNOWS HIS FOOLISHNESS.` · `WHO DOES THE LIFTING?` · then, large: `I, PATRICK, A SINNER.`

segments.voice: If there's paper near you, write three short lines about one part of your story you usually tell as a win. First, what you couldn't do. Then, who or what lifted you. Then, plainly, where you are now. Read it back once, slowly, and notice who turns out to be the hero.
Patrick's Confession. His own account of his life, opening with I, Patrick, a sinner, and told so the gift gets the credit.
Hold onto this: I, Patrick, a sinner. First the honest start, then the thanks. Day sixteen seventy-nine, done.

howItsDone: Christians in Ireland and elsewhere read Patrick's Confession as the saint's own account of his captivity, his calling and his thanks to God.

original.note: Latin: Patrick's word for sinner, from the first line of his Confession.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saint being modest for show.
what it means: he lowers himself so the real hero of the story can be seen: the one who lifted the stone out of the mud.
what a scholar hears: the Confessio's rough Latin, 'peccator rusticissimus', and Paul's 'of whom I am chief' in 1 Timothy 1:15.

chat.says: dad was on shift. asked how the concert went. do i tell him about the crack or just say great?
options: Tell it like Patrick: the crack, the choir that carried you, and what went right.
Just say great. Talking about your mistakes is fishing for sympathy.
Lead with the crack and how bad you were. Humble means only the low parts.
chat.meaning: Patrick tells his weakness plainly, then who lifted him. Humility isn't hiding the bad or only telling it; it's telling it straight and giving credit.

rusticissimus.meaning: Latin: most rustic, the roughest and least polished

Timothy.meaning: a coworker of Paul, who received two letters in the Bible

Dhammapada.meaning: an early collection of the Buddha's sayings in verse

Max Müller.meaning: a scholar who translated the Dhammapada into English
